name: tcms_research
description: Answer a question about Total CMS accurately using this site's own documentation tools. Use this before answering any Total CMS question from memory — the docs served here match the exact version of Total CMS you are talking to.

args.name: question
args.description: What do you want to know about Total CMS? Ask it the way you'd ask a colleague.

body:
The user wants to know: {question}

Answer from this site's documentation, not from memory. Total CMS changes between releases and the docs exposed here are the ones that shipped with this exact install, so they outrank anything you recall.

Work in this order:

1. If the question names a specific Twig function or filter, field type, API endpoint, CLI command, schema option, or extension API, call `docs_lookup` first with the matching `kind`. It returns the structured entry directly — signatures, options, defaults — with no prose to wade through. A near-miss name returns close candidates, so a typo still gets you somewhere.
2. Otherwise call `docs_search` with the key nouns from the question. It returns page `path`s plus the section headings that matched.
3. Call `docs_get` on the most promising `path` to read the full page. Prefer reading one page properly over skimming three.
4. If the first search misses, search again with different terms rather than guessing — Total CMS has its own vocabulary ("collection" not "table", "object" not "row", "schema" not "model", "Site Builder page" not "template").

When you answer, cite the doc path you used so the user can read further. If the documentation genuinely does not cover it, say so plainly instead of filling the gap with a plausible guess — a wrong field name or Twig signature costs the user more time than an honest "the docs don't say."

name: tcms_build_page
description: Plan and build a new Site Builder page in Total CMS — route, template, layout, and data — with field names and Twig signatures verified against this install's documentation. Uses this site's built-in documentation tools.

args.name: purpose
args.description: What is the page for? e.g. 'a case study detail page' or 'a pricing page'.

body:
Help the user build a Total CMS Site Builder page for: {purpose}

Before proposing anything, ground yourself in how Site Builder works on this version. Read `site-builder/overview` with `docs_get`, and use `docs_lookup` with kind `builder_api` for the exact helper signatures — do not guess at `cms.builder.*` names.

The key thing to understand and to explain: there is no build or generate step. A Site Builder page is an object in the `builder-pages` collection, routed at request time. Add the page, it is live.

Work through these decisions with the user:

1. **Route.** A literal path like `/pricing`, or a templated one like `/case-studies/{id}` that resolves against a collection. Templated routes containing placeholders are implicitly pretty — the `prettyUrl` flag only applies to non-templated prefixes. Get this right up front; it is the piece people most often have to redo.
2. **Template.** Which Twig template under `tcms-data/builder/pages/` renders it, and which layout it extends.
3. **Data.** Whether it reads a collection, uses the page's own free-form `data` field (exposed as `page.data.*`), or both.
4. **Navigation and visibility.** Whether it belongs in `cms.builder.nav()`, whether it starts as a draft, and whether it should appear in the sitemap.

Then write the template. Verify every Twig function you use with `docs_lookup` (kind `twig_function` or `twig_filter`) rather than assuming — signatures differ from other CMSs in small ways that fail silently. Use `cms.builder.url(pageId, params)` for internal links so routes stay changeable, and `cms.builder.css/js/asset()` for assets so cache-busting works.

Finish by telling the user exactly where to put each file and how to see it live.

name: tcms_explain_field
description: Explain a Total CMS schema field type — its options, defaults, and how to declare it — from this install's own field reference. Uses this site's built-in documentation tools.

args.name: field_type
args.description: Which field type? e.g. image, deck, card, select, code.

body:
Explain the Total CMS field type: {field_type}

Start with `docs_lookup` using kind `field_type` and that name. The reference index carries the field's real options and defaults; that is the source of truth, not your recollection of similar fields in other systems. If the name is not an exact match, the lookup returns near-misses — offer those rather than inventing a field type that does not exist.

Then use `docs_search` for the prose page covering this field and read it with `docs_get`, so you can explain not just the options but when to reach for it.

Cover, in this order:

1. What the field stores and what it renders as in the admin form builder.
2. Every option it accepts, with defaults and which are required.
3. A complete, copy-pasteable JSON snippet declaring it inside a schema — real option values, not placeholders.
4. How to read the value back out in Twig, since that is the next thing the user will need.
5. Any gotchas the docs call out, especially around nesting (some fields behave differently inside `card` and `deck`).

If the field has close relatives, say briefly when to choose each — most "which field do I use" questions are really that question.

name: tcms_twig_recipe
description: Find the right Total CMS Twig function or filter for a task and write working template code, with signatures verified against this install's Twig reference. Uses this site's built-in documentation tools.

args.name: goal
args.description: What are you trying to do with Twig? e.g. 'list the 5 newest blog posts with thumbnails'.

body:
Write Total CMS Twig for this goal: {goal}

Do not write the template from memory. Total CMS ships a large set of custom Twig functions and filters, and their signatures are specific — a plausible-looking guess usually renders empty rather than erroring, which is the worst kind of wrong.

First, use `docs_lookup` with kind `twig_function` and no `name` to list what exists, and the same with kind `twig_filter`. Scan for the ones that fit the goal, then look each one up by name for its exact signature and arguments. Fill in surrounding concepts with `docs_search` plus `docs_get`.

Two specifics worth checking every time, because they are the most common sources of silently wrong output:

- Use `cms.collection.objects()` to read collection content. The bare `cms.objects()` is a deprecated proxy.
- Image helpers take the object, the image options, and the collection context as separate arguments. Do not merge them into one array.

Then write the complete template — not a fragment. Include the loop, the empty state, and the markup around it, so the user can paste it in and see it work. Comment any line where the Total CMS way differs from stock Twig.

Finally, name the doc paths you used, so the user can go deeper on the pieces they want to change.

name: tcms_troubleshoot_mcp
description: Diagnose why an AI client (Claude, ChatGPT, or another MCP agent) cannot connect to a Total CMS MCP endpoint. Walks the known failure modes in the order they actually occur. Uses this site's built-in documentation tools.

args.name: symptom
args.description: What does the AI client report? e.g. 'connection failed', 'connects but no tools', 'works then 401s'.

args.name: site_url
args.description: Optional. The MCP endpoint URL being connected to, if you know it.

body:
Diagnose a Total CMS MCP connection failure.

Symptom: {symptom}
Endpoint: {site_url}

These failures stack — a site often has two at once, and fixing one reveals the next. Work the list in order rather than jumping to the most interesting hypothesis. Read `mcp/server` with `docs_get` for how the endpoint is meant to behave, and search the docs for anything the symptom names specifically.

1. **Is a bot filter blocking the client before it reaches PHP?** Cloudflare's AI-bot rules block the `Claude-User` agent by default, which returns a 403 or error 1010 that looks exactly like a broken server. Test with `curl -A "Claude-User" <endpoint>` and compare against a normal user agent. If they differ, the fix is in the CDN, not in Total CMS.

2. **Is the `Authorization` header reaching PHP?** Under Apache with PHP-FPM/CGI the header is commonly stripped, so OAuth completes and then every call 401s — the signature symptom being "it authorizes, then nothing works." Total CMS ships an `.htaccess` rule that re-exposes it as `HTTP_AUTHORIZATION`. Confirm the rule is present and that the site is actually using the shipped `.htaccess`.

3. **Is the endpoint URL right for the install layout?** A site in a subfolder serves MCP under that prefix, and discovery lives at `<prefix>/.well-known/mcp.json` rather than the domain root. A URL that is correct for a root install 404s here.

4. **Connects but shows no tools, or fewer than expected?** That is authorization, not connectivity. Tool visibility is scoped by persona: anonymous callers see only what is exposed publicly, and listing versus calling are gated separately — a token with the wrong scope can list a tool and be refused when it calls it. Check whether public MCP access is on and what each collection's own MCP access is set to.

5. **Registration itself rejected?** Some clients request scopes the server does not know. Confirm dynamic client registration succeeded before assuming the transport is at fault.

For each step tell the user what to run, what a healthy result looks like, and what the failure means. Do not recommend disabling security to make a symptom disappear — narrow the cause first, then fix that.

name: tcms_model_collection
description: Design a Total CMS schema and collection for a kind of content — the right field type for every value, help text agents can read, timestamps, and the SEO card — with every type verified against this install's own field reference. Uses this site's built-in documentation tools.

args.name: content
args.description: What kind of content? e.g. 'team members with photos and bios', 'events with dates and venues'.

args.name: edition
args.description: Optional. Standard or Pro — custom schemas need Pro.

body:
Design a Total CMS schema and collection for: {content}
Edition: {edition}

Do not model this from memory. Total CMS ships around forty field types, and the difference between a data model that ages well and one the user fights for years is almost entirely which type each value gets. Custom schemas are a **Pro** edition feature — if this site is on Standard, say so before designing anything, and check whether one of the reserved schemas (`blog`, `image`, `gallery`, `feed`, `podcast-episode`, …) already fits.

**1. Read the reference schema first.** Call `get_schema` with id `totalcms`. That reserved schema demonstrates every built-in field type with its real settings, and each property's help text says what the field is for. Copy property definitions out of it rather than writing them from memory. Verify each type you pick with `docs_lookup` kind `field_type`, and read `schemas/overview` with `docs_get` if the shape is unfamiliar.

**2. Match the field to the shape of the value.** `text` is the last resort, not the default. A date in a text field cannot be filtered by month, a number in a text field sorts as a string, and a yes/no in a text field is a typo waiting to happen.

- the identity / URL slug -> `id` with `"settings": {"autogen": "${title}"}`
- a headline or label -> `text`; a plain summary or note -> `textarea`; a formatted body -> `styledtext`
- a date or a timestamp -> `date` / `datetime`
- yes or no -> `toggle`; one of a fixed list -> `select` (`radio` for two to five shown at once); several of a fixed list -> `checklist`
- tags an editor grows over time -> `list` with `"settings": {"propertyOptions": true}`
- a count, rating or sort order -> `number`; a whole number -> `number` with `"type": "integer"`; money -> `price`
- an email / a URL / a phone -> `email` / `url` / `phone`
- one image / several / a file / a file library -> `image` / `gallery` / `file` / `depot`; a hosted video -> `video`
- a fixed group of related fields (an address, a hero) -> `card`, never flat `addressLine1`, `addressCity`, `addressPostcode`…
- repeating structured items (FAQs, team members, line items) -> `deck` (`deckTable` for short rows), never a `list` or a `json`
- a Twig, HTML or CSS snippet -> `code` with a `mode`; free-form data a template reads -> `json`; an inline SVG -> `svg`
- an API key the site reuses -> `secret`; a password to verify and never read back -> `password`

**Ask what "category" means before modelling it** — it is five different things. Blog-style tags, several per object and editor-extensible, are a `list` with `propertyOptions`. A dropdown of fixed choices is a `select`. Several fixed choices are a `checklist`. Grouping collections in the admin sidebar is the collection's own `category` setting. Grouping schemas in the schema editor is the schema's top-level `category`, where `Internal` is reserved.

**3. Let the field decide the type.** Every property has a `field` (the editor) and a `type` (the stored shape). **Omit `type`** and the saver fills it in from the field — right most of the time. When you want the shipped validation, use a **property reference** instead: `"$ref": "https://www.totalcms.co/schemas/properties/<type>.json"` buys you the pattern for a URL, the format check for an email and the empty-is-allowed branch. Name a type explicitly only when the field's default is wrong for the value — `"type": "integer"` on a `number` that must be whole is the common case. Never hand-write `"type": "string"` on a `code`, `url`, `email`, `json` or `svg` field: it validates, but the schema editor's type dropdown falls out of step and the schema page draws a second, mismatched type icon beside the field icon.

**4. Help text on every property, a description on the schema.** These are not decoration: both feed the MCP catalog that other AI agents read, so generic text there produces generic content later. Write each as a brief to a writer who cannot see the site — not "The title" but "Headline shown in listings and as the page title. Sentence case, under 70 characters, no trailing period." Read `mcp/agent-editing`, section "Writing for agents", for the full set of examples. Every property having help and the schema having a description is the definition of done, not a follow-up.

**5. Add timestamps when dates matter.** They are schema properties, not automatic. A record gets `created` and `updated` only if the schema declares them — `datetime` fields with `"settings": {"onCreate": true}` and `{"onUpdate": true}`. Without them a record seeded by an import has no dates at all: no sitemap `lastmod`, no `datePublished` or `dateModified` in the JSON-LD. Put `updated` in the `index` so the sitemap can read it.

**6. If these objects become pages, add the SEO card.** A `seo` property that is a `card` with `"schemaref": "https://www.totalcms.co/schemas/seo.json"`, a full-width `formgrid` row, **and** `"seo"` in the schema's `index` array — without the index entry the sitemap builders never see noindex, because they read the index rather than the object files. The collection also needs its **URL** set, or its objects get no canonical, no `og:url` and no Article JSON-LD. Read `site-builder/seo` with `docs_get`.

**7. Two layout traps.** A card or a deck needs a whole `formgrid` row (`seo seo`, `address address`); a half cell (`seo .`) collapses the card's own inner grid. Deck item keys are letters, digits and underscores — no hyphens — because items are read in Twig with dot notation (`faqs.q1`, never `faqs['q-1']`). The admin converts as you type; data you write by hand does not get that favour.

Then produce, in full: the complete schema JSON, and the collection settings that go with it — id, name, schema, URL, sort order, sitemap, SEO mapping, and MCP exposure with a real `mcp.description`. Explain the choices that were not obvious, especially anywhere you chose a `card` or `deck` over flat fields.

**Write only after the user confirms.** `create_schema` and `create_collection` are admin tools: they need an API key or an OAuth token with write access. If they are not in your tool list this connection is read-only — hand over the JSON and say where to paste it, rather than discovering it halfway through.

name: tcms_write_content
description: Create or edit an object in a Total CMS collection safely — read the schema's help text as the brief, match the house style, patch rather than replace, and respect each field's stored shape. Uses this site's built-in documentation tools.

args.name: collection
args.description: Which collection? e.g. blog, team, events.

args.name: id
args.description: Optional. An existing object to edit; omit to create a new one.

body:
Write content in the Total CMS collection `{collection}`.

Brief: {brief}
Existing object to edit: {id}

**1. Read the model before writing a word.** Call `describe_collection` on `{collection}` to see which properties are indexed and how the site describes itself to agents, then `get_schema` on its schema and read every property's `help`. **The help text is the brief for that field** — it says what the value is for, what shape it takes, and the constraints the field type cannot imply ("under 70 characters", "usually one category", "future dates schedule it"). Follow it literally. Where help is empty, say so: a field with no brief is a guess, and the fix belongs on the site.

**2. Read a neighbour for house style.** `query_collection` for the most recent few items, then `get_object` on the closest one with `format: "html"`. Match its voice, its length, its heading depth and how it treats the optional fields. Do not invent a new style for a collection that already has one.

**3. Editing? Patch, never replace.** Use `patch_object` with only the fields that change:

    patch_object { collection: "{collection}", id: "{id}", data: { title: "New Title" } }

Omitted fields keep their stored values, so there is nothing to round-trip and nothing to lose. `update_object` is a **full replace** — the server saves exactly the body you send, and every schema field you omit reverts to its default, which silently discards anything you did not think to carry across. Use it only when you mean to rewrite the whole record, and then: fetch with `format: "html"` first (the default `markdown` format *converts* styled text for reading, and writing that back permanently replaces the stored HTML), edit inside the full returned object, strip the `url` key the read tools decorate items with, and send everything.

Three merge rules hold either way. **Containers replace whole** — a card, deck or list value in the payload replaces the stored one entirely, so send the complete container to change any part of it. **Clearing is explicit** — pass `""` or `[]`; omitting a field never clears it. **Binary fields are untouchable** — image, file, gallery and depot values keep what they have, and a payload that sets one is refused.

**4. Respect each field's shape.** A `list` is an array of strings, not a comma-joined line. A `date` or `datetime` is ISO 8601. A `styledtext` field holds HTML — real tags, not markdown. A `textarea` holds plain text with no markup at all. A `select` takes exactly one of its declared options, spelled as declared, and a `checklist` an array of them. A `deck` is a dictionary keyed by item id, and those keys are letters, digits and underscores only. When you have not written a field type before, `docs_lookup` with kind `field_type` gives its stored shape.

**5. Never invent an id.** If the schema's `id` property carries an `autogen` rule, omit `id` and let the server derive it from the source property. If it does not, ask the user what the id should be — a slug is a URL, and they are the ones who have to live with it.

**6. Never write a `password` or `secret` field.** They exist to be verified or read by the site, not authored by an agent. Leave any you find alone, however the brief reads.

**7. Draft first where the schema allows it.** If there is a `draft` toggle or a publish date, use it and tell the user how to go live. A collection with neither publishes the moment you save.

Show the user the exact payload and what it will change, and wait for confirmation before calling `create_object` or `patch_object`. Both are admin tools — if they are absent from your tool list this connection is read-only, so deliver the payload and say where it goes. After a successful write the response echoes the saved object: confirm your change is in it, and do **not** clear the cache — the write fires `object.updated` and the affected pages invalidate themselves.

The whole workflow, including the description slots that shape what agents like you produce, is in `mcp/agent-editing`.

name: tcms_audit_seo
description: Audit a Total CMS site's SEO setup — the Site SEO record, each collection's mapping and URL, and the SEO card on the records that become pages — and report what to fix in priority order. Uses this site's built-in documentation tools.

args.name: collection
args.description: Optional. Audit one collection's pages; omit for the site-wide setup.

body:
Audit the SEO setup of this Total CMS site.
Scope: {collection}

Read `site-builder/seo` with `docs_get` before judging anything. Total CMS resolves every tag at render time from three layers, first non-empty wins:

1. the **SEO card** on the record,
2. the **collection's field mapping**,
3. the **site defaults** on the Site SEO record.

So a value that looks missing on a record is very often being supplied correctly by the layer beneath it. Report a gap only when all three are empty. Work bottom-up.

**Layer 3 — the Site SEO record.** `get_object` on collection `seo-site`, id `seo-site`. If that collection does not exist, it is finding number one — the site has no defaults at all, and `tcms collection:create seo-site` provisions it (the id is reserved, so no schema argument is needed). Then check every field that actually reaches the output: **Site Name**, **Base URL** (nothing gets a canonical without it), the title template and separator, **Default Description**, **Default Social Image** (1200x630), the Twitter handle, **Organization Name**, **Organization Logo** (a real upload, at least 112x112), **Social Profiles** (one absolute URL per line, emitted as `Organization.sameAs`), and **Contact Email** / **Contact URL** — those two become `Organization.email` and a customer-support `ContactPoint`, a trust signal search and answer engines weigh, and they are empty on most sites. Note whether Emit JSON-LD and Emit Social are on; with JSON-LD off, no structured data is written at all.

**Layer 2 — collection mapping and URL.** `list_collections`, then `describe_collection` on each collection whose objects are public pages (or only the one named in the scope above). For each, read the SEO block: Structured Data Type, Title Property, Description Property, Image Property. Know the shipped defaults before calling a mapping missing — a `blog` collection already maps `article` / `title` / `summary` / `image`, a `feed` collection maps `content` as its description, and a saved block merges **over** the defaults one key at a time. The mapping only matters for collections that name their headline, summary or image something else. Then check the collection's **URL**: without it, objects get no canonical, no `og:url` and no Article JSON-LD, which is usually the highest-impact finding on a site.

**Layer 1 — the records.** `get_object` on a representative object or two per collection and read its `seo` card. Is **Title** using `${placeholder}` composition where that would beat a restated headline? Is **Social Title** set where the page title is too long for a share card — it replaces `og:title` and `twitter:title` only, and skips the site title template. Is **Description** written on the card, or falling through to a mapped property that is really a body? Mapped descriptions are flattened and cut at 160 characters; a card-written one is emitted whole. Does **Social Image** resolve, and does the image carry alt text (it becomes `og:image:alt`)? And flag **No Index** wherever it is on: it also drops the record from the sitemaps and strips its canonical, so it is never just a crawler hint.

**The structural check.** For every schema whose objects render as pages, confirm with `get_schema` that it carries the `seo` card (a `card` property with `"schemaref": "https://www.totalcms.co/schemas/seo.json"`), that `formgrid` gives it a whole row — `seo seo`; a half cell like `seo .` collapses the card's inner grid — and that `"seo"` appears in the schema's `index` array. That last one is the quiet failure: without it the card still drives the `<head>`, but the sitemap builders read the collection index, so a noindexed object stays in the sitemap regardless.

**Report as a prioritised list, worst first.** For each finding give what is wrong, the exact field to change and where it lives (Site SEO record / collection setting / schema property / record card), and what the value should be. Separate the findings that need a human decision — site name, brand description, which image — from the mechanical ones.

**Then offer to apply the safe ones.** Record-level values are `patch_object` calls: the Site SEO record's own fields, an `seo` card on an object. Show each payload, one at a time, and get confirmation before sending it. Collection mappings and schema edits are **not** safe to apply unasked — they change how every object in the collection renders — so hand those over as exact instructions instead. And if the admin tools are absent from your tool list, this connection is read-only: say so up front and deliver the whole audit as instructions.
